claim: RUNX1 was recently identified as a novel mutated gene in human luminal breast cancers.
source: RUNX1 encodes a RUNX family transcription factor (TF) and was recently identified as a novel mutated gene in human luminal breast cancers.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to recent sequencing studies mentioned later in the manuscript.

claim: Runx1 is expressed in all subpopulations of murine mammary epithelial cells except the secretory alveolar luminal cells.
source: We found that Runx1 is expressed in all subpopulations of murine mammary epithelial cells (MECs) except the secretory alveolar luminal cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1, including qRT-PCR, IHC staining, and microarray analysis.

claim: Conditional knockout of Runx1 in MECs by MMTV-Cre led to a decrease in luminal MECs.
source: Conditional knockout of Runx1 in MECs by MMTV-Cre led to a decrease in luminal MECs, largely due to a profound reduction in the estrogen receptor (ER)-positive mature luminal subpopulation
evidence: This is supported by FACS analysis data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The decrease in luminal MECs upon Runx1 knockout is largely due to a profound reduction in the ER-positive mature luminal subpopulation.
source: Conditional knockout of Runx1 in MECs by MMTV-Cre led to a decrease in luminal MECs, largely due to a profound reduction in the estrogen receptor (ER)-positive mature luminal subpopulation
evidence: This is supported by FACS analysis data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: The phenotype of reduced ER-positive mature luminal cells upon Runx1 knockout could be rescued by the loss of either Trp53 or Rb1.
source: a phenotype that could be rescued by the loss of either Trp53 or Rb1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: RUNX1 represses Elf5, a master regulatory TF gene for alveolar cells.
source: Mechanistically RUNX1 represses Elf5, a master regulatory TF gene for alveolar cells
evidence: This is supported by ChIP analysis and expression data shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: RUNX1 regulates mature luminal TF/co-factor genes (e.g., Foxa1 and Cited1) involved in the ER program.
source: and regulates mature luminal TF/co-factor genes (e.g., Foxa1 and Cited1) involved in the ER program.
evidence: This is supported by expression analysis and ChIP data shown in Figures 4, 6, and 7.

claim: RUNX1, RUNX2, and RUNX3, and their common non-DNA-binding partner protein CBFβ, form a small family of heterodimeric transcription factors referred to as Core-Binding Factors (CBFs).
source: RUNX1, RUNX2, and RUNX3, and their common non-DNA-binding partner protein CBFβ, form a small family of heterodimeric transcription factors (TFs) referred to as Core-Binding Factors (CBFs) (Speck and Gilliland, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Speck and Gilliland, 2002.

claim: RUNX family transcription factors are master regulators of cell fate determination in blood, bone, and neuron.
source: They are best known as master regulators of cell fate determination in blood, bone, and neuron, respectively (Chuang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chuang et al., 2013.

claim: RUNX1 is a master regulator of hematopoietic stem cells and multiple mature blood lineages.
source: RUNX1 is a master regulator of hematopoietic stem cells and multiple mature blood lineages.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about RUNX1 function in hematopoiesis.

claim: Translocations and mutations involving both RUNX1 and CBFB are frequently found in human leukemias.
source: Translocations and mutations involving both RUNX1 and CBFB are frequently found in human leukemias (Speck and Gilliland, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Speck and Gilliland, 2002.

claim: Recent whole-genome and whole-exome sequencing studies have consistently identified point mutations and deletions of RUNX1 in human luminal breast cancers.
source: In particular, in breast cancer, recent whole-genome and whole-exome sequencing studies have consistently identified point mutations and deletions of RUNX1 in human luminal breast cancers (Banerji et al., 2012; Cancer Genome Atlas Network, 2012; Ellis et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to three sequencing studies.

claim: Mutations in CBFB were also identified in luminal breast cancers.
source: In addition, mutations in CBFB were also identified in luminal breast cancers from these studies.
evidence: This is supported by reference to the same sequencing studies mentioned in the previous sentence.

claim: CBFβ is critical for enhancing DNA-binding by RUNX TFs through allosteric regulation.
source: Its gene product CBFβ is critical for enhancing DNA-binding by RUNX TFs through allosteric regulation (Bravo et al., 2001; Tahirov et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bravo et al., 2001 and Tahirov et al., 2001.

claim: There are two major epithelial cell lineages in the mammary gland: luminal lineage (including ductal and alveolar luminal cells) and basal lineage (the mature cell type in the basal lineage is myoepithelial cell).
source: There are two major epithelial cell lineages in the mammary gland (MG), luminal lineage (including ductal and alveolar luminal cells), and basal lineage (the mature cell type in the basal lineage is myoepithelial cell) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about mammary gland structure, also illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: These two types of MECs are produced by multipotent mammary stem cells (MaSCs, which are basal cells) during embryonic development or upon MEC transplantation to cleared mammary fat pads.
source: These two types of MECs are produced by multipotent mammary stem cells (MaSCs, which are basal cells) during embryonic development or upon MEC transplantation to cleared mammary fat pads (Shackleton et al., 2006; Stingl et al., 2006; Spike et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to three studies.

claim: In adult MGs, MECs appear to be maintained by both lineage-specific unipotent stem cells and multipotent basal MaSCs, based on lineage tracing studies.
source: In adult MGs, they appear to be maintained by both lineage-specific unipotent stem cells and multipotent basal MaSCs, based on lineage tracing studies (Van Keymeulen et al., 2011; van Amerongen et al., 2012; Rios et al., 2014; Tao et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to five lineage tracing studies.

claim: GATA3 has been shown as a master regulator for both ductal and alveolar luminal cells.
source: for example, GATA3 has been shown as a master regulator for both ductal and alveolar luminal cells (Kouros-Mehr et al., 2006; Asselin-Labat et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by citations to two studies.

claim: ELF5 was identified as a master regulator of alveolar cells.
source: ELF5 was identified as a master regulator of alveolar cells (Oakes et al., 2008; Choi et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citations to two studies.

claim: SLUG (SNAIL2) was shown as a master regulator of MaSCs, and it could reprogram differentiated MECs to transplantable MaSCs, together with another TF, SOX9.
source: SLUG (SNAIL2) was shown as a master regulator of MaSCs, and it could reprogram differentiated MECs to transplantable MaSCs, together with another TF, SOX9 (Guo et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Guo et al., 2012.

claim: Runx1 is the predominantly expressed Runx gene in both luminal and basal cells.
source: Results showed that Runx1 is the predominantly expressed Runx gene in both luminal and basal cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: RUNX1 protein is expressed in luminal and basal MECs in adult virgin MGs.
source: Immunohistochemical (IHC) staining further confirmed the expression of RUNX1 protein in these two major MEC types in adult virgin MGs (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by IHC data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: RUNX1 expression is largely absent in alveolar luminal cells that start to emerge during pregnancy.
source: However, RUNX1 expression is largely absent in alveolar luminal cells (ALs) that start to emerge during pregnancy (Figure 1D–E).
evidence: This is supported by IHC data shown in Figures 1D-E.

claim: In the lactating gland, the only MEC type that still expresses RUNX1 is the myoepithelial cell.
source: In the lactating gland, the only MEC type that still expresses RUNX1 is the myoepithelial cell (Figure 1F–G).
evidence: This is supported by IHC data shown in Figures 1F-G.

claim: Upon involution, RUNX1 expression is restored to a pattern resembling that of the virgin gland.
source: Upon involution, RUNX1 expression is restored to a pattern resembling that of the virgin gland (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by IHC data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Microarray expression profiling confirmed Runx1 expression in all MEC subsets except in ALs.
source: Estimation of Runx1 levels based on this microarray dataset confirmed its expression in all MEC subsets except in ALs (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is supported by microarray data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: In pregnant MGs, Runx1 was expressed in basal MECs but not in luminal MECs (mainly ALs).
source: in particular, in the pregnant MGs, Runx1 was also found expressed in basal MECs but not in luminal MECs (mainly ALs) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by microarray data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: qRT-PCR verified that Runx1 was expressed in sorted LPs and MLs but not in Wap-Cre-marked ALs.
source: Lastly, by qRT-PCR, we verified that Runx1 was indeed expressed in sorted LPs and MLs but not in Wap-Cre-marked ALs (Figure 1J).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: Breast cancer-associated missense mutations of RUNX1 either affect amino acid residues that directly contact DNA, or disrupt the overall fold of its DNA-binding RUNT domain or abolish its binding to CBFβ.
source: Based on a previous alanine-scanning site-directed mutagenesis study (Li et al., 2003), we found that these missense mutations either affect amino acid residues in RUNX1 that directly contact DNA, or disrupt the overall fold of its DNA-binding RUNT domain or abolish its binding to CBFβ, both of which would also perturb its DNA-binding (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on inference from a previous mutagenesis study cited (Li et al., 2003) and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The point mutations in RUNX1 lead to loss-of-function due to disrupted DNA-binding ability.
source: Thus, similar to RUNX1 deletions, the point mutations also lead to loss-of-function of RUNX1, due to disrupted DNA-binding ability.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis of mutation effects on DNA binding.

claim: Runx1−/− mice died during mid-gestation mainly due to hemorrhages in the central nervous system.
source: Runx1−/− mice died during mid-gestation mainly due to hemorrhages in the central nervous system and are thus not suitable to determine the effect of Runx1-loss on MG development (Okuda et al., 1996; Wang et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to two studies.

claim: In virgin MGs, MMTV-Cre mainly targeted MECs in the luminal lineage, but it could also lead to Cre-mediated recombination in a portion of basal MECs.
source: Lineage analysis revealed that in virgin MGs, MMTV-Cre mainly targeted MECs in the luminal lineage, but it could also lead to Cre-mediated recombination in a portion of basal MECs (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by FACS analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Loss of Runx1 expression in YFP+ MECs from MMTV-Cre;Runx1L/L;R26Y females was confirmed by qRT-PCR.
source: By fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS), we isolated YFP+ MECs from MMTV-Cre;Runx1L/L;R26Y females and MMTV-Cre;Runx1L/+ and +/+;R26Y control females and by qRT-PCR, we confirmed the loss of Runx1 expression in YFP+ MECs from MMTV-Cre;Runx1L/L;R26Y females (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Whole-mount analysis of MGs from MMTV-Cre;Runx1L/L;R26Y virgin females or dams on lactation day-0 did not reveal any obvious gross morphological abnormalities.
source: Whole-mount analysis of MGs from MMTV-Cre;Runx1L/L;R26Y virgin females or dams on lactation day-0 did not reveal any obvious gross morphological abnormalities, although a portion (3 out of 7) of MMTV-Cre;Runx1L/L;R26Y females exhibited a slight delay in expansion of their ductal trees during pubertal growth (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by whole-mount analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: None of the MMTV-Cre;Runx1L/L;R26Y dams were able to successfully nurse their pups.
source: Surprisingly, however, none of the MMTV-Cre;Runx1L/L;R26Y dams were able to successfully nurse their pups (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by weaning record data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Most pups from MMTV-Cre;Runx1L/L;R26Y dams died within 24 hr postpartum and no milk spots were observed in them.
source: Most of their pups died within 24 hr postpartum and no milk spots were observed in them compared to pups from MMTV-Cre;Runx1+/+(or L/+);R26Y dams.
evidence: This is an observation from the nursing experiments.

claim: MGs of lactating MMTV-Cre;Runx1L/L;R26Y females revealed milk stasis and an increasing number of cytoplasmic lipid droplets.
source: A closer examination of MGs of lactating MMTV-Cre;Runx1L/L;R26Y females revealed milk stasis and an increasing number of cytoplasmic lipid droplets (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The nursing defects observed are most likely due to a disrupted function of RUNX1 in myoepithelial cells.
source: Since Runx1 is only expressed in myoepithelial cells at this stage (Figure 1D–G,I, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), we reasoned that the nursing defects observed are most likely due to a disrupted function of RUNX1 in myoepithelial cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the expression pattern of Runx1 during lactation.

claim: The percentages of the YFP-marked MEC population were significantly reduced in MMTV-Cre;Runx1L/L;R26Y virgin females compared to control females.
source: In MMTV-Cre;Runx1L/L;R26Y virgin females, we found that the percentages of the YFP-marked MEC population (representing Runx1-null MECs) were significantly reduced when compared to those of the MMTV-Cre;Runx1+/+;R26Y control females (Figure 3D–E).
evidence: This is supported by FACS analysis shown in Figures 3D-E.

claim: The ratios of the YFP-marked luminal to basal subsets were significantly reduced in MMTV-Cre;Runx1L/L;R26Y females.
source: Furthermore, the ratios of the YFP-marked luminal to basal subsets were also significantly reduced in MMTV-Cre;Runx1L/L;R26Y females (Figure 3D,F)
evidence: This is supported by FACS analysis shown in Figures 3D and 3F.

claim: The reduction in the YFP+ luminal/basal ratio was most likely due to a reduction in the YFP-marked Runx1-null luminal population.
source: However, since the overall population of YFP+ MECs in MMTV-Cre;Runx1L/L;R26Y females was reduced (Figure 3D–E), the reduction in the YFP+ luminal/basal ratio was most likely due to a reduction in the YFP-marked Runx1-null luminal population.
evidence: This is inferred from the overall reduction in YFP+ MECs.

claim: Most breast cancers, including both basal-like and luminal subtypes, may originate from luminal cells, rather than from basal MaSCs.
source: Recent studies suggest that most breast cancers, including both basal-like and luminal subtypes, may originate from luminal cells, rather than from basal MaSCs (Lim et al., 2009; Molyneux et al., 2010; Proia et al., 2011; Keller et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to four studies.

claim: RUNX1 and CBFB mutations have only been found in the luminal subtype of human breast cancers.
source: Furthermore, RUNX1 and CBFB mutations have only been found in the luminal subtype of human breast cancers (Banerji et al., 2012; Cancer Genome Atlas Network, 2012; Ellis et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citations to three sequencing studies.

claim: GSEA showed significant enrichment of a previously generated LP signature and downregulation of a ML signature in Runx1-null luminal cells.
source: By gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA [Subramanian et al., 2005]), we observed significant enrichment of a previously generated LP signature and downregulation of a ML signature in Runx1-null luminal cells (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Significant enrichment of multiple gene sets related to p53 signaling was observed in Runx1-null luminal cells.
source: Furthermore, we also observed significant enrichment of multiple gene sets related to p53 signaling in Runx1-null luminal cells in relation to Runx1-WT luminal cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), possibly indicating a stress response in these mutant luminal cells in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Elf5 was upregulated in Runx1-null luminal cells.
source: In our microarray data, we found that Elf5, a TF gene critically required in the alveolar cell lineage and a LP marker (Oakes et al., 2008; Choi et al., 2009; Lim et al., 2010), was upregulated in Runx1-null luminal cells
evidence: This is supported by microarray data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Several ductal luminal TF/co-factor genes (e.g., Gata3, Foxa1, Esr1, Cited1) were downregulated in Runx1-null luminal cells.
source: whereas several ductal luminal TF/co-factor genes (e.g., Gata3, Foxa1, Esr1, Cited1) were downregulated (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by microarray data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Expression levels of Foxa1, Esr1, and Cited1 were downregulated in Runx1-null luminal cells by qRT-PCR validation.
source: When validated by qRT-PCR, we found that although the expression of Gata3 did not seem to be significantly affected in luminal cells upon Runx1-loss, expression levels of Foxa1, Esr1, and Cited1 were downregulated in Runx1-null luminal cells, whereas Elf5 expression was upregulated (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Elf5 expression was upregulated in Runx1-null luminal cells by qRT-PCR validation.
source: When validated by qRT-PCR, we found that although the expression of Gata3 did not seem to be significantly affected in luminal cells upon Runx1-loss, expression levels of Foxa1, Esr1, and Cited1 were downregulated in Runx1-null luminal cells, whereas Elf5 expression was upregulated (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The YFP+ Runx1-null CD14−c-Kit− ML subpopulation was significantly reduced in both pubertal and adult virgin MMTV-Cre;Runx1L/L;R26Y females.
source: Intriguingly, we found that in both pubertal and adult virgin MMTV-Cre;Runx1L/L;R26Y females, the YFP+ Runx1-null ML subpopulation defined based on CD14 and c-Kit staining (Lin−CD24+CD29loCD14−c-Kit−, referred to as CD14−c-Kit− MLs hereafter) (Asselin-Labat et al., 2011) was significantly reduced, whereas the YFP+ Runx1-null LP subpopulation (Lin−CD24+CD29loCD14+c-Kit+, referred to as CD14+c-Kit+ LPs hereafter) was increased (Figure 4C–D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: This is supported by FACS analysis shown in Figures 4C-D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: The YFP+ Runx1-null LP subpopulation was increased in both pubertal and adult virgin MMTV-Cre;Runx1L/L;R26Y females.
source: Intriguingly, we found that in both pubertal and adult virgin MMTV-Cre;Runx1L/L;R26Y females, the YFP+ Runx1-null ML subpopulation defined based on CD14 and c-Kit staining (Lin−CD24+CD29loCD14−c-Kit−, referred to as CD14−c-Kit− MLs hereafter) (Asselin-Labat et al., 2011) was significantly reduced, whereas the YFP+ Runx1-null LP subpopulation (Lin−CD24+CD29loCD14+c-Kit+, referred to as CD14+c-Kit+ LPs hereafter) was increased (Figure 4C–D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: This is supported by FACS analysis shown in Figures 4C-D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: Runx1 expression in YFP+ LPs from MMTV-Cre;Runx1L/L;R26Y females was significantly reduced.
source: By qRT-PCR, we found that while Runx1 expression in YFP+ LPs from MMTV-Cre;Runx1L/L;R26Y females was significantly reduced, its expression in YFP-marked MLs was only slightly reduced (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Runx1 expression in YFP-marked MLs from MMTV-Cre;Runx1L/L;R26Y females was only slightly reduced.
source: By qRT-PCR, we found that while Runx1 expression in YFP+ LPs from MMTV-Cre;Runx1L/L;R26Y females was significantly reduced, its expression in YFP-marked MLs was only slightly reduced (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Many YFP+ MLs in MMTV-Cre;Runx1L/L;R26Y females might have escaped Cre-mediated excision in at least one copy of their Runx1L alleles.
source: This data suggested that many YFP+ MLs in MMTV-Cre;Runx1L/L;R26Y females might have escaped Cre-mediated excision in at least one copy of their Runx1L alleles (thus they were either Runx1+/+ or Runx1+/−).
evidence: This is inferred from the qRT-PCR data showing only slight reduction in Runx1 expression in YFP+ MLs.

claim: RUNX1 is essential for the emergence or maintenance of the ML lineage.
source: The data thus also suggests that RUNX1 is essential for the emergence or maintenance of the ML lineage.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that YFP+ MLs appear to have escaped Runx1 deletion.

claim: The luminal cell compartment of the mouse MG can be resolved into non-clonogenic ER+ MLs, as well as clonogenic ER+ LPs and ER− LPs based on CD49b and Sca1 staining.
source: A recent study demonstrated that the luminal cell compartment of the mouse MG could be further resolved into non-clonogenic ER+ MLs, as well as clonogenic ER+ LPs and ER− LPs based on CD49b and Sca1 staining; the ER+ LPs may represent progenitors for ER+ MLs whereas the ER− LPs probably represent alveolar progenitors (Shehata et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Shehata et al., 2012.

claim: The CD49b−Sca1+ ER+ ML subpopulation was significantly reduced in MMTV-Cre;Runx1L/L;R26Y females.
source: We found that compared to their corresponding subpopulations in MMTV-Cre;Runx1+/+;R26Y control females, the CD49b−Sca1+ ER+ ML subpopulation was significantly reduced in MMTV-Cre;Runx1L/L;R26Y females
evidence: This is supported by FACS analysis shown in Figures 4F-G.

claim: The CD49b+Sca1− ER− LP subpopulation was significantly increased in MMTV-Cre;Runx1L/L;R26Y females.
source: whereas the CD49b+Sca1− ER− LP subpopulation was significantly increased
evidence: This is supported by FACS analysis shown in Figures 4F-G.

claim: The CD49b+Sca1+ ER+ LP subpopulation was not significantly altered in MMTV-Cre;Runx1L/L;R26Y females.
source: the CD49b+Sca1+ ER+ LP subpopulation was not significantly altered (Figure 4F–G).
evidence: This is supported by FACS analysis shown in Figures 4F-G.

claim: The YFP-marked ER− LP subset had a profound reduction in Runx1 expression.
source: We found that whereas the YFP-marked ER− LP subset had a profound reduction in Runx1 expression, the YFP+ ER+ LP subset exhibited a partial reduction in Runx1 transcripts, and the YFP+ ER+ ML subpopulation had almost no loss of Runx1 expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G)
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G.

claim: The YFP+ ER+ LP subset exhibited a partial reduction in Runx1 transcripts.
source: We found that whereas the YFP-marked ER− LP subset had a profound reduction in Runx1 expression, the YFP+ ER+ LP subset exhibited a partial reduction in Runx1 transcripts, and the YFP+ ER+ ML subpopulation had almost no loss of Runx1 expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G)
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G.

claim: The YFP+ ER+ ML subpopulation had almost no loss of Runx1 expression.
source: We found that whereas the YFP-marked ER− LP subset had a profound reduction in Runx1 expression, the YFP+ ER+ LP subset exhibited a partial reduction in Runx1 transcripts, and the YFP+ ER+ ML subpopulation had almost no loss of Runx1 expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G)
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G.

claim: RUNX1 is required for the development or maintenance of the ER+ luminal lineage.
source: Collectively, our data suggest that RUNX1 is required for the development or maintenance of the ER+ luminal lineage, and it is particularly essential for the ER+ MLs.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined FACS and expression data.

claim: RUNX1 is particularly essential for the ER+ MLs.
source: Collectively, our data suggest that RUNX1 is required for the development or maintenance of the ER+ luminal lineage, and it is particularly essential for the ER+ MLs.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined FACS and expression data.

claim: Pathway signatures of RB1 mutation, TP53 mutation, and RUNX1 mutation are co-associated with human luminal B breast tumors.
source: Interestingly, one recent sequencing study unveiled that pathway signatures of RB1 mutation, TP53 mutation, and RUNX1 mutation are co-associated with human luminal B breast tumors (Ellis et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ellis et al., 2012.

claim: >50% of luminal breast cancer cases with RUNX1 mutations are accompanied by mutations or deletions in either TP53 or RB1 genes.
source: Furthermore, by carefully examining luminal breast cancer cases with RUNX1 mutations, we noticed that >50% of them are accompanied by mutations or deletions in either TP53 or RB1 genes (Cancer Genome Atlas Network, 2012).
evidence: This is based on analysis of data from Cancer Genome Atlas Network, 2012.

claim: Upon MMTV-Cre-induced Trp53 or Rb1 loss alone, the percentages of YFP-marked MECs increased dramatically.
source: Upon MMTV-Cre-induced Trp53 or Rb1 loss alone, the percentages of YFP-marked MECs increased dramatically so that the majority of MECs in their MGs became YFP+ (Figure 5A, increased from ∼20–30% to ∼70–90%), suggesting a growth advantage for Trp53-null or Rb1-null MECs (in relation to their Trp53-WT or Rb1-WT YFP− neighbors).
evidence: This is supported by FACS analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Trp53-null or Rb1-null MECs have a growth advantage in relation to their WT neighbors.
source: Upon MMTV-Cre-induced Trp53 or Rb1 loss alone, the percentages of YFP-marked MECs increased dramatically so that the majority of MECs in their MGs became YFP+ (Figure 5A, increased from ∼20–30% to ∼70–90%), suggesting a growth advantage for Trp53-null or Rb1-null MECs (in relation to their Trp53-WT or Rb1-WT YFP− neighbors).
evidence: This is inferred from the dramatic increase in YFP+ MECs upon Trp53 or Rb1 loss.

claim: The percentages of the YFP-marked luminal population were reduced upon MMTV-Cre-induced Trp53 or Rb1 loss alone.
source: However, the percentages of the YFP-marked luminal population were both reduced (Figure 5A, middle and bottom left plots compared to upper left plot, green circles).
evidence: This is supported by FACS analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Disruption of Runx1 together with Trp53 significantly increased the percentages of the YFP+ luminal population.
source: Interestingly, disruption of Runx1 either together with Trp53 or with Rb1 significantly increased the percentages of the YFP+ luminal population (Figure 5A–C, increased from ∼4% [Trp53-loss alone] to ∼11% [Runx1/Trp53-loss] [Figure 5B]
evidence: This is supported by FACS analysis shown in Figures 5A-C.

claim: Disruption of Runx1 together with Rb1 significantly increased the percentages of the YFP+ luminal population.
source: Interestingly, disruption of Runx1 either together with Trp53 or with Rb1 significantly increased the percentages of the YFP+ luminal population (Figure 5A–C, increased from ∼4% [Trp53-loss alone] to ∼11% [Runx1/Trp53-loss] [Figure 5B] and from ∼12% [Rb1-loss alone] to ∼23% [Runx1/Rb1-loss] [Figure 5C], respectively).
evidence: This is supported by FACS analysis shown in Figures 5A-C.

claim: The percentage of the YFP-marked ML subpopulation was reverted back to almost the normal level upon simultaneous loss of Runx1 together with either Trp53 or Rb1.
source: Of particular note, the percentage of the YFP-marked ML subpopulation, which was dramatically reduced upon Runx1-loss alone (Figure 5A, upper right plot, red circle), was reverted back to almost the normal level upon simultaneous loss of Runx1 together with either Trp53 or Rb1 (Figure 5A, middle right plot for Trp53 [5B for quantification], bottom right plot for Rb1 [5C for quantification], red circles).
evidence: This is supported by FACS analysis shown in Figures 5A-C.

claim: Abundant ERα+ luminal MECs were detected in both MMTV-Cre;Runx1L/L;Trp53L/L;R26Y and MMTV-Cre;Runx1L/L;Rb1L/L;R26Y compound females.
source: To verify the presence of ER+ MECs in the MGs of these compound female mice, we performed IHC staining for ERα and could indeed detect abundant ERα+ luminal MECs in both MMTV-Cre;Runx1L/L;Trp53L/L;R26Y and MMTV-Cre;Runx1L/L;Rb1L/L;R26Y compound females (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–B
evidence: This is supported by IHC data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: More than 50% reduction in Runx1 expression level was observed in the YFP-marked ML subpopulation sorted from MMTV-Cre;Runx1L/L;Rb1L/L;R26Y females.
source: By qRT-PCR analysis, we observed more than 50% reduction in the Runx1 expression level in the YFP-marked ML subpopulation sorted from MMTV-Cre;Runx1L/L;Rb1L/L;R26Y females (Figure 5D), suggesting a significant portion of these YFP+ MLs should have undergone biallelic excision of their Runx1L alleles.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: A significant portion of YFP+ MLs in MMTV-Cre;Runx1L/L;Rb1L/L;R26Y females should have undergone biallelic excision of their Runx1L alleles.
source: By qRT-PCR analysis, we observed more than 50% reduction in the Runx1 expression level in the YFP-marked ML subpopulation sorted from MMTV-Cre;Runx1L/L;Rb1L/L;R26Y females (Figure 5D), suggesting a significant portion of these YFP+ MLs should have undergone biallelic excision of their Runx1L alleles.
evidence: This is inferred from the >50% reduction in Runx1 expression.

claim: RUNX1 knockdown stable lines could only be obtained from TP53-mutant T47D cells but not from TP53-WT MCF7 cells.
source: Interestingly, despite multiple attempts, we were only able to obtain RUNX1 knockdown (kd) stable lines from TP53-mutant T47D cells but not from TP53-WT MCF7 cells.
evidence: This is an observation from cell culture experiments.

claim: A similar genetic interaction between RUNX1-loss and TP53-loss may also operate in human ER+ luminal breast cells.
source: This observation suggests that a similar genetic interaction between RUNX1-loss and TP53-loss may also operate in human ER+ luminal breast cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the inability to obtain RUNX1 knockdown in TP53-WT cells.

claim: Upon RUNX1 knockdown in T47D cells, the protein level of ELF5 was increased.
source: By Western blot, we found that upon RUNX1 kd, the protein level of ELF5 was increased, whereas the protein levels of both ERα and FOXA1 were reduced, and CITED1 protein level appeared unchanged (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Upon RUNX1 knockdown in T47D cells, the protein levels of both ERα and FOXA1 were reduced.
source: By Western blot, we found that upon RUNX1 kd, the protein level of ELF5 was increased, whereas the protein levels of both ERα and FOXA1 were reduced, and CITED1 protein level appeared unchanged (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Upon RUNX1 knockdown in T47D cells, CITED1 protein level appeared unchanged.
source: By Western blot, we found that upon RUNX1 kd, the protein level of ELF5 was increased, whereas the protein levels of both ERα and FOXA1 were reduced, and CITED1 protein level appeared unchanged (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: RUNX1 was shown as a direct target of ELF5 and is repressed by it, based on chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) analysis.
source: Interestingly, it was shown previously that RUNX1 is a direct target of ELF5 and is repressed by it, based on chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) analysis (Kalyuga et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kalyuga et al., 2012.

claim: A largely opposite expression pattern of Elf5 and Runx1 was observed in microarray data for sorted MEC subsets.
source: In our microarray data for sorted MEC subsets, as well as those publicly available microarray datasets we analyzed, we could always observe a largely opposite expression pattern of Elf5 and Runx1 (Figure 1I, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by microarray data shown in Figure 1I and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: In basal cells and MLs in which Runx1 is highly expressed, Elf5 is not expressed.
source: In both basal cells and MLs in which Runx1 is highly expressed, Elf5 is not; Elf5 expression is greatly elevated in ALs whereas Runx1 expression is repressed.
evidence: This is supported by microarray data shown in Figure 1I and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Elf5 expression is greatly elevated in ALs whereas Runx1 expression is repressed.
source: In both basal cells and MLs in which Runx1 is highly expressed, Elf5 is not; Elf5 expression is greatly elevated in ALs whereas Runx1 expression is repressed.
evidence: This is supported by microarray data shown in Figure 1I and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Upon induction of alveolar differentiation in HC11 cells, the ELF5 protein level was increased, whereas the RUNX1 protein level was reduced.
source: This negative correlation in their expression levels could be further confirmed in the HC11 cell line model. While both Runx1 and Elf5 were expressed in uninduced HC11 cells, upon induction of alveolar differentiation, the ELF5 protein level was increased, whereas the RUNX1 protein level was reduced (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Significant binding of RUNX1 to multiple evolutionary conserved RUNX-binding sites in the ELF5 locus was identified by ChIP analysis.
source: To determine whether ELF5 is also a direct target of RUNX1, we performed ChIP analysis on T47D cells and identified significant binding of RUNX1 to multiple evolutionary conserved RUNX-binding sites in the ELF5 locus (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: RUNX1-binding was particularly profound in an enhancer region ∼17 kb upstream of the ELF5 transcription start site (ECR-1).
source: The RUNX1-binding was particularly profound in an enhancer region ∼17 kb upstream of the ELF5 transcription start site (ECR-1, Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Significant binding of RUNX1 to the −1.6 kb and −1.9 kb motifs in the FOXA1 locus was confirmed by ChIP assay.
source: By ChIP assay, we confirmed significant binding of RUNX1 to the −1.6 kb and −1.9 kb motifs in the FOXA1 locus (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: FOXA1 and ELF5 genes may be direct targets of RUNX1 positively and negatively regulated by it, respectively.
source: Collectively, these data suggest that FOXA1 and ELF5 genes may be direct targets of RUNX1 positively and negatively regulated by it, respectively.
evidence: This is inferred from the ChIP and expression data.

claim: Both Elf5 and Esr1 appeared upregulated in ER+ LPs and ER+ MLs from Rb1/Runx1 double mutants compared to Rb1 single mutants.
source: When comparing double mutants (with Rb1/Runx1-loss) to single mutants (with Rb1-loss alone), we found that both Elf5 and Esr1 appeared upregulated in ER+ LPs and ER+ MLs (based on CD49 and Sca1 staining) from double mutants (Figure 7A–B, left plots)
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figures 7A-B.

claim: Foxa1 and Cited1 were downregulated in the rescued double mutant ER+ MLs compared to Rb1 single mutants.
source: and Foxa1 and Cited1 were downregulated in the rescued double mutant ER+ MLs (Figure 7B, left plot).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Both Elf5 and Esr1 were upregulated in ER+ LPs and ER+ MLs from double mutants compared to WT females.
source: From this comparison, we found that both Elf5 and Esr1 were also upregulated and Foxa1 and Cited1 were slightly downregulated in ER+ LPs and ER+ MLs from double mutants (Figure 7A–B, right plots).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figures 7A-B.

claim: Foxa1 and Cited1 were slightly downregulated in ER+ LPs and ER+ MLs from double mutants compared to WT females.
source: From this comparison, we found that both Elf5 and Esr1 were also upregulated and Foxa1 and Cited1 were slightly downregulated in ER+ LPs and ER+ MLs from double mutants (Figure 7A–B, right plots).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figures 7A-B.

claim: In Runx1-mutant ER+ LPs, both Elf5 and Esr1 were upregulated and Foxa1 and Cited1 also appeared slightly upregulated.
source: Interestingly, we found that in Runx1-mutant ER+ LPs both Elf5 and Esr1 were upregulated and Foxa1 and Cited1 also appeared slightly upregulated (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In older Rb1-null single mutants, Esr1, Foxa1, and Cited1 were upregulated and Elf5 was downregulated in their YFP+ CD14−c-Kit− MLs.
source: By using this strategy, we found that in Rb1-null single mutants (controls), Esr1, Foxa1, and Cited1 were upregulated and Elf5 was downregulated in their YFP+ CD14−c-Kit− MLs when they aged
evidence: This is supported by time course qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: In YFP+ MLs from double mutants, following Runx1 reduction, although Esr1 was upregulated to a similar level, Foxa1 and Cited1 were not, and Elf5 was even further upregulated.
source: however, in YFP+ MLs from double mutants, following Runx1 reduction, although Esr1 was upregulated to a similar level (to that of single mutants), Foxa1 and Cited1 were not, and Elf5 was even further upregulated (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by time course qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: A similar trend of changes for Foxa1, Cited1, and Elf5 was observed in YFP+ CD14+c-Kit+ LPs from the same animals.
source: We also observed a similar trend of changes for Foxa1, Cited1, and Elf5 in YFP+ CD14+c-Kit+ LPs from the same animals (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by time course qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: In ER+ luminal cells, RUNX1 negatively and positively regulates the expression of Elf5 and mature luminal TF/co-factor genes (e.g., Foxa1 and Cited1), respectively.
source: Overall, the data from this time course study further supports that in ER+ luminal cells, RUNX1 negatively and positively regulates the expression of Elf5 and mature luminal TF/co-factor genes (e.g., Foxa1 and Cited1), respectively.
evidence: This is inferred from the time course expression data.

claim: Differentiation of ER+ luminal MECs requires coordinated expression of these factors and Runx1-loss may disrupt their coordinated expression.
source: This expression pattern suggests that differentiation of ER+ luminal MECs requires coordinated expression of these factors and Runx1-loss may disrupt their coordinated expression.
evidence: This is inferred from the expression pattern data.

claim: Elf5 is a key target gene of RUNX1 repressed by it in MECs.
source: Collectively, our in vitro and in vivo expression analyses coupled with ChIP analysis suggest that Elf5 is a key target gene of RUNX1 repressed by it in MECs.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined ChIP and expression data.

claim: Foxa1 is a direct target of RUNX1.
source: RUNX1 also positively regulates the expression of mature luminal TF/co-factor genes involved in the ER program and among them, Foxa1 is a direct target of RUNX1
evidence: This is inferred from ChIP data showing RUNX1 binding to FOXA1 regulatory regions.

claim: RUNX1 does not appear to regulate transcription of Esr1 directly.
source: and RUNX1 does not appear to regulate transcription of Esr1 directly.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of consistent downregulation of Esr1 in vivo and the pattern of Esr1 upregulation.

claim: GATA3 has been shown as a common master regulator for both ER+ ductal luminal cells and ER− alveolar luminal cells.
source: Among TFs that control cell fates of the two subpopulations of luminal MECs, GATA3 has been shown as a common master regulator for both ER+ ductal luminal cells and ER− alveolar luminal cells (Kouros-Mehr et al., 2006; Asselin-Labat et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by citations to two studies.

claim: ELF5 has been identified as a key regulatory TF specific for the alveolar luminal subset.
source: whereas ELF5 has been identified as a key regulatory TF specific for the alveolar luminal subset (Oakes et al., 2008; Choi et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to two studies.

claim: RUNX1 is a key regulator of ER+ luminal MECs.
source: In this study, we identified RUNX1 as a key regulator of ER+ luminal MECs.
evidence: This is the main conclusion inferred from all the experimental data presented.

claim: RUNX1 controls the in vivo fate of ER+ luminal cells by repressing the program for an alternative cell fate choice (i.e., repressing the key TF gene for alveolar cells, Elf5).
source: RUNX1 controls the in vivo fate of this luminal subpopulation by repressing the program for an alternative cell fate choice (i.e., repressing the key TF gene for alveolar cells, Elf5)
evidence: This is inferred from the ChIP and expression data showing RUNX1 represses Elf5.

claim: RUNX1 controls the in vivo fate of ER+ luminal cells by optimizing activation of the ML gene expression program (i.e., regulating key mature luminal TF/co-factor genes such as Foxa1).
source: and by optimizing activation of the ML gene expression program (i.e., regulating key mature luminal TF/co-factor genes such as Foxa1) (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is inferred from the ChIP and expression data showing RUNX1 regulates Foxa1.

claim: Loss of Runx1 impairs the fate of ER+ luminal cells, leading to a profound reduction in this luminal subpopulation.
source: Loss of Runx1 impairs the fate of ER+ luminal cells, leading to a profound reduction in this luminal subpopulation.
evidence: This is supported by FACS data showing reduction in ER+ luminal cells upon Runx1 loss.

claim: The loss of either Trp53 or Rb1 can rescue the defect caused by Runx1 loss, leading to hyperproliferation of Runx1-mutant ER+ luminal cells.
source: However, the loss of either Trp53 or Rb1 can rescue this defect, leading to hyperproliferation of Runx1-mutant ER+ luminal cells, which may eventually progress to ER+ luminal breast cancer, upon acquisition of additional mutations (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by FACS data showing rescue of ER+ luminal cells in double mutants.

claim: Runx1-mutant ER+ luminal cells may eventually progress to ER+ luminal breast cancer, upon acquisition of additional mutations.
source: However, the loss of either Trp53 or Rb1 can rescue this defect, leading to hyperproliferation of Runx1-mutant ER+ luminal cells, which may eventually progress to ER+ luminal breast cancer, upon acquisition of additional mutations (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the rescue data and human cancer mutation patterns.

claim: RUNX1 and ELF5 are two master regulators for mutually exclusive cell fate choices (i.e., ductal vs alveolar fates) by antagonizing each other's transcription program.
source: Thus, combined with the previous observation in which RUNX1 was reciprocally shown as a direct target repressed by ELF5 (Kalyuga et al., 2012), these data suggest that RUNX1 and ELF5 are two master regulators for mutually exclusive cell fate choices (i.e., ductal vs alveolar fates) by antagonizing each other's transcription program (e.g., RUNX1 promotes the ER program [this study], whereas ELF5 suppresses it [Kalyuga et al., 2012]) (Figure 8A)
evidence: This is inferred from the mutual repression between RUNX1 and ELF5.

claim: RUNX1 not only represses Elf5 expression in ER+ luminal cells but also in all other MEC subsets in which Runx1 is expressed.
source: Intriguingly, RUNX1 not only represses Elf5 expression in ER+ luminal cells but also in all other MEC subsets in which Runx1 is expressed (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: In basal MECs where Elf5 is normally not expressed, loss of Runx1 led to its profound upregulation.
source: Strikingly, in basal MECs where Elf5 is normally not expressed (Figure 1I, Figure 1—figure supplement 1), loss of Runx1 led to its profound upregulation (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: In normal MGs, RUNX1 represses expression of Elf5 in almost all MEC subsets in which Runx1 is expressed.
source: These data suggest that in normal MGs, RUNX1 represses expression of Elf5 in almost all MEC subsets in which Runx1 is expressed.
evidence: This is inferred from the widespread de-repression of Elf5 upon Runx1 loss.

claim: RUNX1 protein expression correlates with poor prognosis in ER− breast cancer and more specifically in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC).
source: Recently it was found that RUNX1 protein expression correlates with poor prognosis in ER− breast cancer and more specifically in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) (Ferrari et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ferrari et al., 2014.

claim: RUNX1 was found associated with super-enhancers in an ER− breast cancer cell line.
source: Furthermore, RUNX1 was also found associated with super-enhancers in an ER− breast cancer cell line (Hnisz et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hnisz et al., 2013.

claim: RUNX1 may play an oncogenic role in ER− breast cancers.
source: these recent findings suggest that RUNX1 may also play an oncogenic role in ER− breast cancers.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation with poor prognosis and association with super-enhancers.

claim: SNAI2 (encodes SLUG) is a target of ELF5 repressed by it.
source: The link between RUNX1 and ELF5 in basal MECs may explain a potential oncogenic role of RUNX1 in ER− breast cancer/TNBC, as it was shown previously that SNAI2 (encodes SLUG) is a target of ELF5 repressed by it (Chakrabarti et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chakrabarti et al., 2012.

claim: Snai2-null mice exhibit a nursing defect, due to failed milk ejection caused by defects in basal/myoepithelial cell differentiation.
source: Interestingly, it was shown recently that Snai2-null mice exhibit a nursing defect, due to failed milk ejection caused by defects in basal/myoepithelial cell differentiation (Phillips et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Phillips et al., 2014.

claim: In Runx1-null mice, upregulation of Elf5 in basal MECs may lead to repression of Snai2, which may provide an explanation for the similar nursing defect.
source: In Runx1-null mice, upregulation of Elf5 in basal MECs may lead to repression of Snai2, which may provide an explanation for the similar nursing defect we have observed in our Runx1 conditional knockout mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation based on the known relationships between these factors.

claim: RUNX1 plays a key role in luminal breast cancer as a tumor suppressor in ER+ ductal luminal cells, which may be their cells of origin.
source: In luminal breast cancer, our study provides strong evidence to support that RUNX1 plays a key role in this breast cancer subtype as a tumor suppressor in ER+ ductal luminal cells, which may be their cells of origin.
evidence: This is the main conclusion inferred from all the experimental data.

claim: RUNX3 is a tumor suppressor as it is often inactivated in human breast cancers and loss of one copy of Runx3 led to spontaneous mammary tumor development in a portion of aged female mice.
source: Among them, RUNX3 is also a tumor suppressor as it is often inactivated in human breast cancers and loss of one copy of Runx3 led to spontaneous mammary tumor development in a portion of aged female mice (Huang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Huang et al., 2012.

claim: The tumor suppressor role of RUNX3 in breast cancer is explained by its ability to inhibit ERα-dependent transactivation by reducing the stability of ERα.
source: The tumor suppressor role of RUNX3 in breast cancer is explained by its ability to inhibit ERα-dependent transactivation by reducing the stability of ERα (Huang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Huang et al., 2012.

claim: RUNX2 mainly exhibits oncogenic roles in breast cancer by promoting invasiveness and metastasis via its target, SNAI2.
source: In contrast, RUNX2 mainly exhibits oncogenic roles in breast cancer by promoting invasiveness and metastasis via its target, SNAI2 (Chimge et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chimge et al., 2011.

claim: RUNX2 may also play a tumor suppressor role in breast cancer by antagonizing ERα.
source: however it may also play a tumor suppressor role in breast cancer by antagonizing ERα (thus, similar to RUNX3) (Chimge et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chimge et al., 2012.

claim: RUNX1 has been shown as a novel tethering factor for recruiting ERα to its genomic sites for ER-mediating transcriptional activation.
source: Furthermore, RUNX1 has also been shown as a novel tethering factor for recruiting ERα to its genomic sites for ER-mediating transcriptional activation (Stender et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Stender et al., 2010.

claim: Estrogen signaling has dual roles in MECs and breast cancer cells; on one hand it has an oncogenic role by promoting proliferation of ER+ luminal breast cancer cells, on the other hand it also has a tumor suppressor role by promoting MEC differentiation and inhibiting metastasis of breast cancer cells.
source: Estrogen signaling has dual roles in MECs and breast cancer cells; on one hand it has an oncogenic role by promoting proliferation of ER+ luminal breast cancer cells, on the other hand it also has a tumor suppressor role by promoting MEC differentiation and inhibiting metastasis of breast cancer cells (Chimge and Frenkel, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chimge and Frenkel, 2013.

claim: RUNX1 was found among a 17-gene signature associated with metastasis as a gene downregulated in metastasis-prone solid tumors, including breast cancer.
source: The tumor suppressor role of RUNX1 is also consistent with a previous observation in which RUNX1 was found among a 17-gene signature associated with metastasis as a gene downregulated in metastasis-prone solid tumors, including breast cancer (Ramaswamy et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ramaswamy et al., 2003.

claim: The loss of Runx1 does not appear to affect transcription of Esr1 directly.
source: We show that the loss of Runx1 does not appear to affect transcription of Esr1 directly (thus, the affected luminal cells remain phenotypically ER+)
evidence: This is inferred from the expression and ChIP data.

claim: Loss of Runx1 may lead to a crippled ER program, in part due to de-repression of Elf5 and insufficient upregulation of Foxa1.
source: but may lead to a crippled ER program, in part due to de-repression of Elf5 and insufficient upregulation of Foxa1, which may reduce the sensitivity and output of ER signaling, respectively (Hurtado et al., 2011; Kalyuga et al., 2012).
evidence: This is inferred from the expression data and supported by citations.

claim: The impaired ER program in Runx1-mutant ER+ luminal cells may cause cellular stress, leading to activation of the p53 pathway and subsequently cell cycle arrest and/or apoptosis.
source: The impaired ER program in Runx1-mutant ER+ luminal cells may cause cellular stress, leading to activation of the p53 pathway and subsequently cell cycle arrest and/or apoptosis; as a result, abnormally differentiated Runx1-mutant ER+ luminal cells are outcompeted by their WT neighbors in vivo.
evidence: This is a speculative model based on the GSEA data showing p53 pathway enrichment.

claim: The loss of Trp53 or Rb1 can relieve the cell cycle arrest or positively activate cell cycle, respectively, and/or rescue apoptosis in Runx1-mutant ER+ luminal cells.
source: However, the loss of Trp53 or Rb1 can relieve the cell cycle arrest or positively activate cell cycle, respectively, and/or rescue apoptosis in them, leading to rescue of the Runx1-mutant ER+ luminal cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue data in double mutants.

claim: In humans, RUNX1/TP53-mutant or RUNX1/RB1-mutant ER+ premalignant luminal cells may progress to ER+ luminal breast cancer, upon acquisition of additional oncogenic events.
source: In humans, upon acquisition of additional mutations, the RUNX1/TP53-mutant or RUNX1/RB1-mutant ER+ premalignant luminal cells may progress to ER+ luminal breast cancer, upon acquisition of additional oncogenic events (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is a speculative model based on the mouse data and human mutation patterns.

claim: Germline mutations of RUNX1 that result in haploinsufficiency of RUNX1 can lead to an autosomal dominant disorder referred to as familial platelet disorder with a propensity to acute myeloid leukemia (FPD/AML).
source: Of note, germline mutations of RUNX1 that result in haploinsufficiency of RUNX1 can lead to an autosomal dominant disorder referred to as familial platelet disorder with a propensity to acute myeloid leukemia (FPD/AML) (Song et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Song et al., 1999.

claim: In one study that characterized three FPD/AML pedigrees, one female patient with FPD/AML also developed a breast cancer 2 years after AML was diagnosed.
source: Interestingly, in one study that characterized three FPD/AML pedigrees, it was found that one female patient with FPD/AML also developed a breast cancer 2 years after AML was diagnosed, and no other tumors were observed in all three pedigrees (Preudhomme et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Preudhomme et al., 2009.

claim: Germline mutations of RUNX1 may predispose FPD/AML patients to luminal breast cancer, but only under a background of either TP53 or RB1 loss.
source: Although the sample size for this study was too small, it certainly raises an intriguing question as to whether germline mutations of RUNX1 predispose FPD/AML patients to luminal breast cancer, but only under a background of either TP53 or RB1 loss.
evidence: This is a speculative question raised based on the case report and the study's findings.

claim: Loss of RUNX1 may contribute to the development of ER+ luminal breast cancer under a background of either TP53 or RB1 loss and upon cooperation with other additional oncogenic events.
source: In summary, we identified RUNX1 as a key regulator of the ER+ luminal lineage. Loss of RUNX1 may contribute to the development of ER+ luminal breast cancer under a background of either TP53 or RB1 loss and upon cooperation with other additional oncogenic events.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, inferred from all the experimental data.
